qs.q: Why is Ductal Carcinoma In Situ (DCIS) frequently detected on routine screening mammograms?
o: Central cell death leads to visible calcifications
The cancer cells lose E-cadherin and form aggregates
It causes immediate skin dimpling and retraction
qs.e: DCIS is found on mammograms because cells in the centre of the ducts die and calcify, producing visible calcifications. LCIS, by contrast, does not cause calcifications and is invisible on imaging.
qs.s: Breast Carcinoma: Understanding Types, Receptors & Treatment: MCQs

qs.q: What specific microscopic architecture defines the cribriform pattern of Ductal Carcinoma In Situ?
o: Central parts of the duct dying and becoming necrotic
True fibrovascular cores forming branching fronds
Cells forming round cookie-cutter spaces in ducts
Small finger-like projections without a blood vessel
qs.e: The cribriform pattern of DCIS is characterized by cells forming round cookie-cutter like spaces inside the duct. Comedo pattern features central necrosis, whereas micropapillary lacks a central blood vessel.
qs.s: Breast Carcinoma: Understanding Types, Receptors & Treatment: MCQs

qs.q: In the context of bladder pathology, which of the following is a characteristic feature of carcinoma in situ (CIS) on cystoscopy?
o: Calcified nodule within the bladder wall
Mucosal reddening or granularity without a mass
qs.e: CIS presents on cystoscopy as mucosal reddening, granularity, or thickening without an intraluminal mass. Papillary masses are characteristic of papillary carcinomas, and grape-like clusters suggest sarcoma botryoides.
qs.s: Bladder Cancer & Urothelial Neoplasms: Types, Risks, Pathogenesis: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following mammographic features is most characteristic of ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) and serves as the primary method of its detection?
qs.e: DCIS is almost always detected on mammography by the presence of microcalcifications resulting from necrosis or secretions within the ducts. Unlike invasive carcinomas, it rarely forms a distinct palpable desmoplastic mass.
qs.s: Breast Cancer Guide: Epidemiology, Risk Factors & Classification: MCQs

qs.q: A 52-year-old woman undergoes routine screening. A biopsy reveals lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS). Which of the following molecular alterations is most fundamentally responsible for the dyscohesive cellular morphology seen in this lesion?
o: Overexpression of estrogen and progesterone receptors
Loss of E-cadherin expression due to CDH1 mutation
Inactivating mutation of the tumor suppressor gene TP53
Amplification of the HER2 gene on chromosome 17q
qs.e: LCIS is characterized by biallelic loss of the CDH1 gene encoding E-cadherin, leading to a loss of cell-to-cell adhesion and a dyscohesive appearance. Amplification of HER2 is typical of the HER2 molecular pathway rather than LCIS.
qs.s: Breast Cancer Guide: Epidemiology, Risk Factors & Classification: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following architectural patterns of ductal carcinoma in situ is characterized by central necrosis accompanied by calcification and is typically associated with a higher histologic grade?
qs.e: The comedo pattern of DCIS features central necrosis with calcification and represents a higher-grade lesion. Cribriform and micropapillary patterns have different architectural features without the central necrotic zone.
qs.s: Breast Cancer Guide: Epidemiology, Risk Factors & Classification: MCQs

qs.q: A 50-year-old woman undergoes breast conservation therapy for low-grade ductal carcinoma in situ. If left completely untreated, what is the approximate annual rate of progression from this in situ lesion to invasive carcinoma?
qs.e: Untreated low-grade ductal carcinoma in situ progresses to invasive cancer at a rate of approximately 1 percent per year. Higher progression rates would overestimate the indolent nature of untreated low-grade in situ disease.
qs.s: Breast Cancer Guide: Epidemiology, Risk Factors & Classification: MCQs

qs.q: A 58-year-old woman is found to have lobular carcinoma in situ incidentally on a breast biopsy performed for another reason. What is the expected mammographic appearance of this lesion?
qs.e: Lobular carcinoma in situ is almost always incidental, lacking calcifications or mammographic density, which makes its incidence unchanged by screening mammography. Pleomorphic microcalcifications are instead characteristic of high-grade ductal in situ lesions.
qs.s: Breast Cancer Guide: Epidemiology, Risk Factors & Classification: MCQs
